section_summary: This section concludes a translated Japanese War Ministry pamphlet advocating propaganda, expanded military and civil aviation, economic regimentation, and comprehensive national-defense preparedness. It then assembles U.S. diplomatic reports, internal memoranda, cross-references, correspondence, and press clippings concerning Japanese maneuvers, patriotic military propaganda, Army influence in Manchuria and relations with the Soviet Union, personnel disputes, and public fundraising for armaments. The final documents focus on the removal of General Jinsaburō Masaki and the assassination of Major General Tetsuzan Nagata as evidence of factional and political tensions within the Japanese Army.

subfiles.title: Continuation of “Principles of National Defense and Proposals for Its Strengthening”
subfiles.from: Press Bureau, Japanese Ministry of War
subfiles.about: The concluding portion advocates systematic propaganda, stronger air power, economic regimentation, wartime mobilization, and national unity around defense.
subfiles.summary: The pamphlet uses First World War propaganda organizations to argue that modern conflict includes organized struggles over ideas. It contrasts Japanese military and aviation capacity with that of the Soviet Union, China, the United States, and European powers, then calls for expanded military and civil aviation. Its final sections criticize individualistic economics, demand preparations for a controlled wartime economy, and urge the population to organize itself around national defense.

subfiles.title: Despatch D-674 transmitting report on Japanese garrison maneuvers, file copy 1
subfiles.from: F. P. Lockhart, American Consul General, Tientsin
subfiles.about: Lockhart transmits a copy of despatch L-825 concerning Japanese garrison maneuvers.
subfiles.summary: The one-page covering despatch forwards Lockhart's report to the American Legation. Its enclosure is identified as despatch L-825 of November 23, 1934.

subfiles.title: Despatch L-825 on maneuvers of the Japanese garrison, enclosure copy 1
subfiles.from: F. P. Lockhart, American Consul General, Tientsin
subfiles.to: C. E. Gauss, American Chargé d'Affaires ad interim, Peiping
subfiles.about: Lockhart confirms planned Japanese troop maneuvers in the Tangshan–Luan County area.
subfiles.summary: The report confirms information supplied in despatch L-824 about the dates and locality of forthcoming maneuvers. Troops were to travel by train, and Lockhart characterized the movement as part of normal autumn training.

subfiles.title: Despatch D-674 transmitting report on Japanese garrison maneuvers, file copy 2
subfiles.from: F. P. Lockhart, American Consul General, Tientsin
subfiles.about: A duplicate covering despatch transmits L-825 on Japanese garrison maneuvers.
subfiles.summary: This is another file copy of Lockhart's transmittal to the Department of State. It identifies the enclosed Legation despatch as L-825.

subfiles.title: Despatch L-825 on maneuvers of the Japanese garrison, enclosure copy 2
subfiles.from: F. P. Lockhart, American Consul General, Tientsin
subfiles.to: C. E. Gauss, American Chargé d'Affaires ad interim, Peiping
subfiles.about: A duplicate enclosure confirms routine Japanese autumn maneuvers by troops sent into the Tangshan–Luan County area.
subfiles.summary: The page duplicates L-825 and refers back to L-824. It states that the troop transfer by rail was part of the garrison's normal autumn training activities.

subfiles.title: Despatch D-674 transmitting report on Japanese garrison maneuvers, file copy 3
subfiles.from: F. P. Lockhart, American Consul General, Tientsin
subfiles.about: A further copy of D-674 forwards Lockhart's maneuver report to Washington.
subfiles.summary: The despatch contains only the formal transmittal of L-825 to the Secretary of State. It notes that the underlying report was addressed to the Legation.

subfiles.title: Despatch L-825 on maneuvers of the Japanese garrison, enclosure copy 3
subfiles.from: F. P. Lockhart, American Consul General, Tientsin
subfiles.to: C. E. Gauss, American Chargé d'Affaires ad interim, Peiping
subfiles.about: Lockhart reports confirmation of the Japanese garrison's autumn field maneuvers.
subfiles.summary: The despatch says Japanese troops would be carried by train to the Tangshan–Luan County area. It treats the exercise as ordinary seasonal training rather than an exceptional deployment.

subfiles.title: Despatch D-674 transmitting report on Japanese garrison maneuvers, file copy 4
subfiles.from: F. P. Lockhart, American Consul General, Tientsin
subfiles.about: Another file copy forwards despatch L-825 on Japanese garrison maneuvers.
subfiles.summary: This duplicate cover letter records the formal transmission of the maneuver report. It gives the same enclosure and distribution information as the other copies.

subfiles.title: Despatch L-825 on maneuvers of the Japanese garrison, enclosure copy 4
subfiles.from: F. P. Lockhart, American Consul General, Tientsin
subfiles.to: C. E. Gauss, American Chargé d'Affaires ad interim, Peiping
subfiles.about: A duplicate copy reports confirmed Japanese autumn maneuvers and associated rail movements.
subfiles.summary: Lockhart confirms that the troops mentioned in L-824 would maneuver in the previously reported area and on the stated dates. Their transport was described as a normal part of autumn training.

subfiles.title: Despatch D-674 transmitting report on Japanese garrison maneuvers, file copy 5
subfiles.from: F. P. Lockhart, American Consul General, Tientsin
subfiles.about: A fifth surviving copy of the cover despatch transmits report L-825.
subfiles.summary: The document is another administrative transmittal of the Japanese garrison maneuver report. It repeats the enclosure identification and copy instructions.

subfiles.title: Despatch L-825 on maneuvers of the Japanese garrison, enclosure copy 5
subfiles.from: F. P. Lockhart, American Consul General, Tientsin
subfiles.to: C. E. Gauss, American Chargé d'Affaires ad interim, Peiping
subfiles.about: The final duplicate enclosure confirms maneuvers in the Tangshan–Luan County area.
subfiles.summary: The report confirms the location and timing of the Japanese exercise. Lockhart again explains that troops would travel by train and that the activity was ordinary autumn training.

subfiles.title: Division memorandum on Kobe despatch 411 and “Japan's Army and Navy”
subfiles.from: Division of Far Eastern Affairs, Department of State
subfiles.about: An internal review characterizes Japan's Army and Navy as patriotic and anti-American military propaganda.
subfiles.summary: The memorandum says the book is typical of contemporary Japanese propaganda intended to generate enthusiasm for the armed forces and war. It highlights its treatment of the United States as a potential enemy and notes introductions by Hayashi, Ōsumi, Araki, and Okada.

subfiles.title: Despatch 411: Book entitled “Japan's Army and Navy”
subfiles.from: Howard Donovan, American Consul, Kobe
subfiles.about: Donovan transmits and analyzes Hirata Shinsaku's patriotic book Japan's Army and Navy, with translated excerpts on Pacific naval rivalry.
subfiles.summary: The translated passages portray the Pacific as Japan's natural sphere and depict American bases and fleet concentration as an encirclement and invasion threat. They defend Japanese naval expansion from the Sea of Okhotsk to the Equator, discuss British, Dutch, Chinese, and Soviet naval forces, and present the Japanese Navy as guardian of Asian peace. Donovan notes possible use of similar material in private schools and forwards the only available copy for inspection.

subfiles.title: Cross-reference sheet for Harbin Political Report 53
subfiles.from: Harbin (Adams)
subfiles.about: The sheet directs researchers to a Harbin report on the increase of Japanese Army power.
subfiles.summary: This filing note cross-references Political Report Harbin 72, report 53. Its stated subject is the growing power of the Japanese Army.

subfiles.title: Duplicate cross-reference sheet for Harbin Political Report 53
subfiles.from: Harbin (Adams)
subfiles.about: A duplicate filing sheet references the Harbin report on increased Japanese Army power.
subfiles.summary: The document repeats the reference information found on page 271. It identifies report 53 as concerning the increase of Japanese Army power.

subfiles.title: Extract: Increase of Japanese Army power
subfiles.from: Adams, Harbin
subfiles.about: The extract assesses favorable Japanese-community reaction in Harbin to the Army's defense pamphlet and political ambitions.
subfiles.summary: Japanese residents in northern Manchuria reportedly approved the Army pamphlet and tended to favor military over civilian political control. The report also links the Army's successful campaign for greater influence to the Kwantung police dispute and the Manchukuo petroleum monopoly.

subfiles.title: Cross-reference sheet for despatch 1090 on annual Army maneuvers
subfiles.from: Japan (Joseph C. Grew)
subfiles.about: The sheet references a report on Japan's annual Army maneuvers and rumored personnel changes.
subfiles.summary: The note records that approximately 50,000 troops participated in November maneuvers. It also points to rumors of forthcoming changes in senior Army personnel.

subfiles.title: Extract from despatch 1090: The Army
subfiles.from: Joseph C. Grew, United States Ambassador to Japan
subfiles.about: The extract reports large annual maneuvers and rumors that General Minami would replace General Hishikari in command of the Kwantung Army.
subfiles.summary: About 50,000 troops took part in maneuvers on November 11–13, with the unusually large number of participants being the chief noteworthy feature. Newspaper rumors predicted Hishikari's transfer to the Supreme War Council and Jirō Minami's appointment as Kwantung Army commander.

subfiles.title: Cross-reference sheet for interview with Japanese War Minister
subfiles.from: Germany (White)
subfiles.about: The sheet references a Völkischer Beobachter interview in which General Hayashi advocated national regimentation for an expected war.
subfiles.summary: The filing note characterizes Hayashi's remarks as favoring organized national preparation for seemingly inevitable conflict. It observes that this message suited the political lesson Nazi propagandists wished to draw.

subfiles.title: Cross-reference sheet for Times comment on Manchukuo expenditure
subfiles.from: Great Britain (Atherton)
subfiles.about: The sheet points to British press comment urging Japan to reduce Army expenditure in Manchukuo.
subfiles.summary: The filing note references a report on commentary in The Times. That commentary warned the Japanese government about excessive military spending in Manchukuo.

subfiles.title: Division memorandum on Peiping despatch 3279
subfiles.from: Division of Far Eastern Affairs, Department of State
subfiles.about: The memorandum summarizes a conference of reactionary Japanese officers at Dairen and their complaints against Chiang Kai-shek and China.
subfiles.summary: The attending officers reportedly criticized Chiang Kai-shek and alleged Chinese failures to implement provisions connected with the Tangku Truce. The memorandum suggests that the statements might have been intended either to intimidate China or to weaken Chiang and hasten Chinese political disintegration. It notes that most cited transport, communications, and customs provisions appeared largely fulfilled.

subfiles.title: Despatch 3279: Japanese Military Conference at Dairen
subfiles.from: C. E. Gauss, American Chargé d'Affaires ad interim, Peiping
subfiles.about: Gauss reports on a meeting of reactionary Japanese officers and examines their accusations that China had not honored the Tangku Truce.
subfiles.summary: The conference included Doihara, Itagaki, and Kagesa, while the more moderate Shibayama was absent. Press reports linked their complaints to Chiang Kai-shek and to alleged failures involving air service, telegraph and telephone links, through freight, and customs. Gauss finds that most practical obligations had already been substantially fulfilled and considers the complaints potentially part of a campaign to intimidate China or undermine Chiang.

subfiles.title: Kenneth Colegrove to Stanley K. Hornbeck requesting the Army pamphlet
subfiles.from: Kenneth Colegrove, Northwestern University
subfiles.to: Stanley K. Hornbeck, Department of State
subfiles.about: Colegrove asks to borrow the Japanese Army pamphlet Principles of National Defense and Proposals for Its Strengthening or an English translation.
subfiles.summary: Colegrove explains that efforts to obtain the pamphlet through other Japanese-material sources had failed. He wished to study it for a proposed World Peace Foundation book on Japanese foreign policy.

subfiles.title: Stanley K. Hornbeck to Kenneth Colegrove concerning access to the Army pamphlet
subfiles.from: Stanley K. Hornbeck, Department of State
subfiles.about: Hornbeck declines to lend the official translation but offers on-site access or private copying at Colegrove's expense.
subfiles.summary: Hornbeck says the Department possesses a forty-eight-page translation attached to an official Embassy report and therefore cannot circulate it privately. He invites Colegrove to consult it during a visit to Washington and suggests that unofficial copying might be arranged for no more than ten dollars.

subfiles.title: Cross-reference sheet on proposed munitions manufacture at the Konan plant
subfiles.from: Seoul (Langdon)
subfiles.about: The sheet references a report that Japanese Army contacts approached Goedicke about manufacturing electrochemical products used in munitions.
subfiles.summary: The proposed work concerned several chemical products required for armaments production at the Konan industrial plant. The underlying report is filed under a separate economic or industrial classification.

subfiles.title: Cross-reference sheet on proposed extension of the Ford assembly plant
subfiles.from: Yokohama (Boyd)
subfiles.about: The sheet references military opposition to Ford's attempt to purchase land for expansion of its Yokohama assembly plant.
subfiles.summary: Ford reportedly tried to acquire additional municipal land for an enlarged assembly operation. The Yokohama municipality refused to sell at the insistence of Japanese military authorities.

subfiles.title: Tsingtao Japanese community fund for purchase of an airplane
subfiles.from: Samuel Sokobin, American Consul, Tsingtao
subfiles.to: Nelson Trusler Johnson, American Minister, Peiping
subfiles.about: Sokobin reports a drive among Japanese residents of Tsingtao to raise ¥45,000 for a scout airplane for the Japanese government.
subfiles.summary: Organizers planned to canvass the approximately 15,000-member Japanese community and close subscriptions on Navy Day, the anniversary of the Battle of the Japan Sea. The proposed aircraft was to be named Tsingtao and presented as an act of requiting the homeland. Sokobin interprets the campaign as evidence that expatriate Japanese believed their position in China required exceptional military strength.

subfiles.title: Report 7699: Japanese garrison prisons and Army Enlightenment Corps
subfiles.from: John [surname illegible], Captain of Infantry, Assistant Military Attaché
subfiles.about: The report lists Japanese garrison prisons and detention stations, prisoner totals, and the Army's disciplinary or Enlightenment Corps at Himeji.
subfiles.summary: Nineteen facilities are listed at divisional or colonial-army headquarters across Japan, Korea, Taiwan, and the Kwantung territory, with a distinction between convicted prisoners and soldiers awaiting trial. Statistical data are said to show a steady decline in prisoner numbers. The Himeji disciplinary barracks received repeat military offenders but excluded men convicted of crimes involving moral turpitude.

subfiles.title: Cross-reference sheet for despatch 1331 on the Army and the Soviet Union
subfiles.from: Japan (Joseph C. Grew)
subfiles.about: The sheet references a discussion of Japanese military attitudes toward the Soviet Union and the Army's political role.
subfiles.summary: This filing note points to despatch 1331. Its subject combines Soviet-Japanese relations with the domestic political influence of the Japanese Army.

subfiles.title: Despatch 1331: Soviet-Japanese Relations—Attitude of the Japanese Military
subfiles.from: Joseph C. Grew, United States Ambassador to Japan
subfiles.about: Grew analyzes why the Japanese Army remained hostile to a broad settlement with the Soviet Union despite improving bilateral relations.
subfiles.summary: The despatch distinguishes the Army's conventional responsibility for defending Manchukuo from its extraordinary domestic political role and constitutional independence. Grew argues that budgetary ambitions, the need for an external menace, and resistance to restrictions on military freedom encouraged continuing anti-Soviet propaganda. Reports of Soviet railways, fortifications, aircraft, submarines, and activity in Xinjiang and Mongolia supported the campaign, leaving Hirota limited to settling individual disputes rather than negotiating a general pact.

subfiles.title: Cross-reference sheet for telegram 151 on General Masaki
subfiles.from: Japan (Joseph C. Grew)
subfiles.about: The sheet references Masaki's removal as Director General of Military Education following a dispute over Army personnel changes.
subfiles.summary: Masaki reportedly objected to personnel changes proposed by the Minister of War. His removal was therefore treated as a significant Army leadership development.

subfiles.title: Telegram 151 on the removal of General Masaki
subfiles.from: Joseph C. Grew, United States Embassy, Tokyo
subfiles.about: Grew reports Masaki's removal and Hirota's private interpretation of the episode as evidence of gradually strengthening government control.
subfiles.summary: Masaki was relieved after opposing Army personnel changes approved by the War Minister and Prince Kan'in. Hirota told Grew that the incident demonstrated the government's slow, step-by-step effort to establish control and thanked the United States for avoiding official questions during the North China crisis. Grew offered to raise any Department views informally in a forthcoming final conversation with Hirota.

subfiles.title: Telegram 166 on the assassination of Major General Nagata
subfiles.from: Edwin L. Neville, United States Embassy, Tokyo
subfiles.about: Neville reports the War Office explanation of Nagata's assassination by Lieutenant Colonel Aizawa.
subfiles.summary: The War Office portrayed Aizawa as personally dissatisfied with reassignment as a military instructor in Formosa, reducing initial fears of a clash between Army factions. The press supported strong punishment, and Lieutenant General Imai was announced as Nagata's successor in the Military Affairs Bureau.

subfiles.title: Cross-reference sheet for despatch 1414 on the removal of General Masaki
subfiles.from: Japan (Edwin L. Neville)
subfiles.about: The filing sheet points to despatch 1414 on General Masaki's removal; the following page is a departmental divider.
subfiles.summary: The reference directs readers to a more detailed report under another decimal-file classification. Its stated subject is the removal of General Masaki.

subfiles.title: Kenneth Colegrove to Stanley K. Hornbeck requesting a second Army pamphlet
subfiles.from: Kenneth Colegrove, Northwestern University
subfiles.to: Stanley K. Hornbeck, Department of State
subfiles.about: Colegrove asks whether he may pay for a trusted person to copy a translation of the 1935 pamphlet We Must Prepare for the National Emergency.
subfiles.summary: Colegrove identifies the publication as a March 1935 product of the Japanese War Department Press Bureau. He acknowledges that Department policy may prevent fulfillment of the request.

subfiles.title: “The New Army Pamphlet: Degeneration of the National Spirit Is Deplored—The Barbarous West”
subfiles.from: The Japan Chronicle
subfiles.about: The clipping summarizes a Japanese War Office pamphlet issued for the thirtieth anniversary of the Russo-Japanese War.
subfiles.summary: The pamphlet presents Japan's crisis as a combination of global unrest and domestic corruption caused by Western individualism, materialism, and weakened national spirit. It condemns imperialist powers and the League of Nations, praises Japan-Manchukuo cooperation, and claims Japan possesses a superior state-centered ethic capable of guiding humanity. The article notes that the Army exercised greater caution after controversy over its previous social and political prescriptions.

subfiles.title: Department of State reply to Kenneth Colegrove concerning the 1935 pamphlet
subfiles.from: Stanley K. Hornbeck, Department of State
subfiles.about: Hornbeck explains that the Department lacks the pamphlet or a translation but encloses a press summary.
subfiles.summary: The reply identifies Colegrove's requested work with The Determination of the Japanese Nation at the Time of Crisis that Marks the Thirtieth Anniversary of the Russo-Japanese War, reportedly issued on February 25, 1935. Because the Department had received neither the original nor a translation, Hornbeck supplied a Japan Advertiser clipping summarizing it.

subfiles.title: Cross-reference sheet for despatch 1427 on Masaki and Watanabe
subfiles.from: Japan (Edwin L. Neville)
subfiles.about: The sheet references a report on Masaki's removal and replacement by General Jōtarō Watanabe.
subfiles.summary: The filing note identifies Masaki's former office as Inspector General of Military Education. It names Watanabe as his replacement.

subfiles.title: Extract: Removal of General Jinsaburō Masaki and appointment of General Jōtarō Watanabe
subfiles.from: Edwin L. Neville, United States Embassy, Tokyo
subfiles.about: The extract analyzes Masaki's removal, Army personnel policy, and Watanabe's appointment as Inspector General of Military Education.
subfiles.summary: Hayashi removed Masaki because of disagreements over promotions and assignments as well as older political and personal antagonisms. Contemporary reports suggested that conservative, professionally oriented officers were being favored over politically adventurous officers, although the changes remained internal to the Army rather than a civilian imposition. Watanabe publicly disapproved of military participation in politics, while the Supreme Military Council called for tighter internal control after the controversy.

subfiles.title: Division memorandum reviewing Tokyo despatch 1450
subfiles.from: Division of Far Eastern Affairs, Department of State
subfiles.about: The memorandum evaluates the Embassy's detailed report on Nagata's assassination in light of Hayashi's subsequent resignation.
subfiles.summary: The reviewer finds that despatch 1450 adds little to the earlier telegram announcing the assassination. Hayashi's later resignation is treated as evidence that his effort to create a disciplined, politically disengaged Army faced substantial obstacles.

subfiles.title: Despatch 1450: Assassination of Major General Nagata
subfiles.from: Edwin L. Neville, American Chargé d'Affaires ad interim, Tokyo
subfiles.about: Neville provides a detailed account of Nagata's murder and its possible relationship to factional opposition within the Army.
subfiles.summary: Lieutenant Colonel Saburō Aizawa attacked Nagata with a knife in his War Ministry office on August 12, after which Nagata was posthumously promoted and Aizawa arrested. Official emphasis on Aizawa's resentment over reassignment to Taiwan quickly eased public fear that the murder represented organized factional conflict. Neville nevertheless notes consultations among Hayashi, Prince Kan'in, Araki, and Masaki and concludes that opponents might exploit the killing to obstruct efforts to depoliticize and discipline the Army.

subfiles.title: Despatch transmitting Frankfurter Zeitung article on the killing of General Nagata
subfiles.from: William E. Dodd, United States Ambassador to Germany
subfiles.about: Dodd transmits a translated German newspaper article explaining the background to Nagata's murder.
subfiles.summary: The cover despatch identifies the source as the August 16 issue of the Frankfurter Zeitung. The translated enclosure, which follows outside this section, concerns the killing of General Nagata and the circumstances behind it.
